title: Observed versus Expected
subtitle: how many readmissions should a clinic have had?
name: ModelInMotion_LogisticFE_E03_ObservedVersusExpected

segments.visual: Cedar's twenty risk chips, the expected bar at 8.0 and the eight observed chips, as Episode 2 left them.

sentences.text: Last time, we gave every patient a probability, added them up for Cedar, and got 8 expected readmissions. Cedar had exactly 8.
sentences.say: Last time, we gave every patient a probability, added them up for Cedar, and got eight expected readmissions. Cedar had exactly eight.

segments.visual: A loop arrow runs from Cedar's observed chips back up to its own slices.

sentences.text: A perfect match. But a hollow one.
Those probabilities were built from Cedar's own results. We compared Cedar with itself.

segments.visual: The slices empty; the question appears.

sentences.text: To judge a clinic, the expected number has to come from somewhere else.
So the real question is: expected, according to whom?

segments.visual: Series logo and wordmark; arc and episode title.

sentences.text: Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: observed, versus expected.

segments.visual: Five clusters of chips, one per clinic, in their colours.

sentences.text: Here's a first idea. Pour all five clinics together: 103 patients.
sentences.say: Here's a first idea. Pour all five clinics together: one hundred and three patients.

segments.visual: The chips lose their colours and sort into a lower-risk block of 57 and a higher-risk block of 46, readmitted first.

sentences.text: Sort them by risk, and forget which clinic they came from.
13 of the 57 lower-risk patients were readmitted: 23%.
sentences.say: Thirteen of the fifty-seven lower-risk patients were readmitted: twenty-three percent.

sentences.text: And 29 of the 46 higher-risk patients: 63%.
sentences.say: And twenty-nine of the forty-six higher-risk patients: sixty-three percent.

segments.visual: Two large risk chips with slices of 23% and 63%: the pooled standard.

sentences.text: Call that the pooled standard: what happens to a typical patient of each kind.

segments.visual: Alder's thirty patients twice: on the left as outcomes, on the right as risk chips carrying the standard's slices.

sentences.text: Now take Alder's 30 patients. On the left, what happened to them.
sentences.say: Now take Alder's thirty patients. On the left, what happened to them.

sentences.text: On the right, the slice the standard gives each one.

segments.visual: The slices pour into one dashed bar on a scale of patients: 9.3.

sentences.text: Add up the slices: 24 small ones and 6 large ones come to about 9.3.
sentences.say: Add up the slices: twenty-four small ones and six large ones come to about nine point three.

sentences.text: That's Alder's expected count: what these same patients would produce at a typical clinic.

segments.visual: The thirteen readmitted chips line up on the same scale; a bracket marks +3.7; a small balance tips; the ratio 1.40 appears.

sentences.text: Alder actually had 13.
That's 3.7 more than expected. Or, as a ratio, 13 over 9.3: 1.4.
sentences.say: That's three point seven more than expected. Or, as a ratio, thirteen over nine point three: one point four.

segments.visual: Five rows, one per clinic: observed chips above a dashed expected bar, with the ratio at the right.

sentences.text: Now do the same for all five clinics.

segments.visual: Birch's row lights up: 14 against 16.5, ratio 0.85.

sentences.text: Birch had 14, against 16.5 expected: a ratio of 0.85. Fewer than expected.
sentences.say: Birch had fourteen, against sixteen and a half expected: a ratio of zero point eight five. Fewer than expected.

segments.visual: Raw rates appear beside Alder and Birch: 43% and 47%, the opposite order to the ratios.

sentences.text: Remember the league table? Birch's raw rate was higher than Alder's.
Measured against what their own patients were expected to do, Birch comes out ahead.

segments.visual: A totals line: expected 42.0, observed 42.

sentences.text: And notice: the expected counts add up to 42, exactly the number observed.
sentences.say: And notice: the expected counts add up to forty-two, exactly the number observed.

sentences.text: Against a pooled standard, the clinics as a whole always break even.

segments.visual: The pooled lower-risk block again, this time in clinic colours.

sentences.text: It looks like we're done. But look at where that standard came from.

segments.visual: Alder's 24 chips are bracketed; its 8 readmitted chips pulse.

sentences.text: Of the 57 lower-risk patients in the pool, 24 are Alder's own. And they supplied 8 of the 13 readmissions.
sentences.say: Of the fifty-seven lower-risk patients in the pool, twenty-four are Alder's own. And they supplied eight of the thirteen readmissions.

segments.visual: Alder's chips leave the pool: 23% becomes 15%. Below, Alder's expected bar shortens from 9.3 to 7.2 and its ratio rises to 1.80.

sentences.text: Take Alder out, and the lower-risk rate drops from 23% to 15%.
sentences.say: Take Alder out, and the lower-risk rate drops from twenty-three percent to fifteen.

sentences.text: Alder has been measured against a standard it pushed up itself. Against everyone else, its ratio is not 1.4, but 1.8.
sentences.say: Alder has been measured against a standard it pushed up itself. Against everyone else, its ratio is not one point four, but one point eight.

segments.visual: A log-odds ruler; the pooled step from lower to higher risk, times 5.8.

sentences.text: There's a second, subtler problem: the risk rule itself.
In the pool, higher risk multiplies the odds by 5.8.
sentences.say: In the pool, higher risk multiplies the odds by five point eight.

segments.visual: Four more steps, one per clinic in its colour: times 10, 10, 6 and 5.9; then the within-clinic summary, times 7.5.

sentences.text: But compare patients inside the same clinic, and the gap is wider: 10 at Alder, 10 at Dune, about 6 at Cedar and at Birch.
sentences.say: But compare patients inside the same clinic, and the gap is wider: ten at Alder, ten at Dune, about six at Cedar and at Birch.

sentences.text: Taken together, about seven and a half.

segments.visual: Guides show the pooled step starting near Alder's lower-risk patients and ending near Birch's higher-risk ones.

sentences.text: Why the difference? Most higher-risk patients are at Birch, which does well. Most lower-risk patients are at Alder, which doesn't.
The pool mixes up how sick patients are with where they were treated.

segments.visual: Three recap cards, each with a small icon.

sentences.text: Let's gather it up.
Expected is a sum of probabilities, taken over a clinic's own patients.
Observed minus expected is the evidence. Observed over expected is the ratio.
And both are only as fair as the standard behind them.

segments.visual: Two requirements appear as lines of text.

sentences.text: A fair standard needs two things: a risk rule learned from patients who share a clinic, and a yardstick no single clinic can bend.

segments.visual: Five parallel lines in the clinics' colours on a log-odds panel; the next episode title.

sentences.text: Next time, we get both, with one small change: every clinic gets a number of its own.

segments.visual: Series end card with the next episode title.

sentences.text: This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
